150.bp: When you ask an AI assistant a question while browsing the web, it looks up information to give you better answers. But the web is constantly changing, and most systems rely on old snapshots taken months ago. This matters because outdated information leads to wrong advice, and mixing sources from different trustworthiness levels leaves you vulnerable to mixing fact with fiction.
150.wh: The challenge is that web assistants can't easily let you say 'only check my company intranet' or 'only use news from the last week.' Systems are built with one fixed index of web pages that stays the same unless someone manually rebuilds it. So you have no control over whether an answer comes from a reliable source, and you can't know if the information is stale.
150.ap: OwlerLite lets you define reusable scopes—groups of specific web pages or sources you trust. When you ask a question, you pick which scope to use. Behind the scenes, a crawler continuously watches the pages in your scopes, looking for meaningful changes (not just formatting tweaks). When real changes happen, only those pages get re-indexed. The system then ranks search results by how relevant they are to your question, whether they match your chosen scope, and how recent they are.
150.ww: This works because it closes the trust gap and time gap at once. You control *which* sources the AI sees (trust), and the system knows which sources are freshly updated (recency). Watching for semantic changes means the system doesn't waste effort re-indexing unchanged pages. Combining these three signals—relevance, scope, and freshness—means your answers come from exactly the places you want and the information is current.
150.po: Built as a browser extension, OwlerLite gives you assistants you can actually trust. You can confidently ask about your company's internal policies, know your market research is current, or verify news without mixing yesterday's rumors with today's facts. The payoff is speed and confidence: you get reliable, up-to-date answers without manually hunting sources yourself.

151.bp: Predicting how things will change over time—stock prices, website traffic, power consumption—is crucial for making smart decisions. When you track thousands of related quantities at once (like temperature in different rooms of a building), the patterns get much harder to spot, and computers slow down dramatically.
151.wh: Time series forecasting gets complicated when you have many channels (separate variables to track). The obvious approach tries to learn how each channel influences every other channel, but if you have thousands of channels, that becomes impossibly expensive to compute. Even when you do figure out the relationships, the model often mixes up local patterns (neighbors influence each other) with global patterns (distant variables have distant effects), confusing the prediction.
151.ap: CRAFT reorders the channels like rearranging books on a shelf so similar ones sit together—using an energy-based method to find the lowest-energy arrangement. Then it uses a Transformer model that handles local relationships separately from global ones. Local fusion focuses on neighboring channels in the reordered sequence; global fusion looks at broader relationships. This separation keeps computation manageable even with thousands of channels.
151.ww: Grouping similar channels reduces noise because the model doesn't have to guess wildly about how a random distant channel affects your prediction. Separating local from global patterns lets the model allocate its computation wisely—spending effort on what matters locally (a room's temperature depends heavily on adjacent rooms) and globally (climate patterns affect all rooms the same way). The energy-based reordering acts like a map that makes these dependencies obvious.
151.po: CRAFT scales to datasets with thousands of channels while staying fast enough to be practical. For large-scale web applications tracking many metrics at once—datacenter resource use, user engagement across regions, supply chain inventory—this means accurate predictions without waiting hours for a model to run.

152.bp: Machine learning models learn to recognize patterns by building internal numerical representations of data. These representations should capture what matters (the thing you care about predicting) and throw away noise. When representations work well, they transfer to new tasks; when they fail, the model overfits to irrelevant details.
152.wh: Researchers have discovered that high-dimensional representations often suffer from a weird flaw: important information clusters in a tiny subspace, while most dimensions fill up with noise. Imagine a building where all the important offices occupy one floor and the rest is empty corridors—the space is used inefficiently. This 'spectral imbalance' hurts how well the model generalizes to new problems.
152.ap: SDE uses matrix decomposition (singular value decomposition) to automatically sort each dimension into three bins: strong signals (dimensions carrying task-critical information), weak signals (dimensions with side information), and noise (irrelevant dimensions). Then it selectively amplifies the strong signal dimensions using a curriculum—gradually increasing emphasis as training progresses. It also trains the model to match representations both in the original feature space and after inspecting their mathematical structure.
152.ww: By sorting dimensions rather than treating them equally, the model learns which parts of its representation actually matter. Amplifying strong signals while leaving weak signals and noise alone is like turning up the volume on a radio station you care about. The curriculum prevents training instability that could happen if you suddenly amplified too much. Dual-domain training ensures the representation is geometrically sound in multiple ways.
152.po: Models trained with SDE show better transfer to new tasks and more reliable predictions. For transfer learning tasks common in industry—building a detector trained on one dataset that works on entirely different data—this approach significantly improves both accuracy and robustness.

153.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products or content you might like based on what you and others have interacted with. When the system understands both what items are (product features) and who you are (your interests), it makes better suggestions. But building a real understanding of 'who you are' from clicks alone is hard.
153.wh: Systems usually know a lot about items because they're described in structured databases—a movie's genre, cast, release date. But they struggle with users. You might click the same item for different reasons: a recipe because you're cooking versus a recipe because you're meal-planning. This user-side knowledge is scattered across your history and hard to gather systematically. Also, most people click very few things, making patterns hard to see.
153.ap: SEDIRec uses large language models to interpret your clicking history and infer what you actually care about—not just 'you clicked this recipe' but 'you're interested in quick weeknight meals.' It combines this user-side understanding with item descriptions and collaborative signals (what similar users liked). Then it generates two comparison views using diffusion models with semantic transitions: one highlighting user information and one highlighting item information. Each view is transformed into a collaborative space, and the system learns to match these views.
153.ww: Language models excel at reading between the lines of human behavior, so using them to infer interests is more honest than just counting clicks. Diffusion models gradually morph between different semantic spaces, which helps the system understand how information should transform while learning. Training the model to match user and item views simultaneously ensures these two types of information support each other rather than contradicting.
153.po: The payoff is especially strong for users with sparse histories—people who have clicked few things. Because the system understands their interests semantically (what they *mean* to click) rather than just pattern-matching similar users, it can suggest relevant things even when the direct data is thin.

154.bp: People spend a lot of time copying text from what they're reading, pasting it into a chat interface, typing a question, and then switching back to their work. This stops your flow. It would be faster if an AI assistant just appeared on-screen and explained whatever you selected.
154.wh: Building this is tricky because the assistant needs to know *what you want*. If you highlight a word, do you want a definition, a translation, or background on the concept? Different situations call for different responses. The assistant also needs to learn your preferences—maybe you like concise explanations for technical terms but lengthy context for historical events. Standard chat interfaces assume you explicitly type out your intent each time.
154.ap: Swen is a desktop tool that sits quietly until you select text and press a hotkey. It automatically recognizes whether you want a translation, a concept explanation, or a summary—intent detection that happens without you typing anything. It maintains a user profile that remembers facts about you (your background, your usual preferences for response length or style). Each time you use it, the profile gets richer and your answers become more personalized.
154.ww: Intent detection works because many text selections have patterns: a phrase in another language suggests translation; an unfamiliar term suggests explanation; a long paragraph suggests summarization. The system learns these patterns. Maintaining a profile means the assistant doesn't start from scratch with every interaction—it remembers that you prefer technical depth or simple language, reducing back-and-forth.
154.po: The result is a dramatic speed-up in knowledge lookup during your actual work. Instead of switching apps three times to understand one phrase, you press a hotkey and have the answer instantly. For people doing research, coding, or writing, this is a direct time-saving that keeps you in flow.

155.bp: Graph neural networks are tools for finding patterns in networks—social connections, molecular structures, recommendation graphs. They work by having each node look at its neighbors and learn from them. But some networks have a problem: neighbors are often *different* from each other, not similar.
155.wh: Most graph neural networks assume neighborhoods are homogeneous—similar nodes connect to similar nodes. This assumption breaks in real networks where different things attract (a villain connects to a hero, a protein pairs with its opposite). When neighbors are different, the network learns poorly because it's trying to solve the wrong problem. Worse, a network trained on data where neighbors are dissimilar performs terribly on new data where they're similar, and vice versa.
155.ap: IVQ-GNN tackles this by learning connection patterns—the specific neighborhood structures that actually occur—rather than just measuring homophily or heterophily as a single number. In a pre-training phase, it builds a codebook of these patterns like a dictionary. During fine-tuning, it uses a self-attention mechanism to combine patterns from the codebook, letting it adapt to rare or unseen patterns. This two-stage approach means it can handle both common and unusual network structures.
155.ww: Connection patterns are the real information. By learning and combining specific patterns rather than assuming a uniform structure, the model becomes flexible. The codebook acts as an orthogonal basis—think of it like a mathematical coordinate system for neighborhoods—so the model can accurately express any real pattern by combining these basis vectors. This is more honest than forcing all networks into one assumption.
155.po: IVQ-GNN maintains strong performance across datasets with mixed neighborhood types and improves robustness when encountering unusual connection patterns. For real-world applications—protein interaction networks, social graphs, knowledge graphs—networks are rarely pure homophilous or heterophilous, so this flexibility directly improves accuracy.

156.bp: Online communities have millions of posts daily. Moderators must decide what stays and what gets removed, enforcing community rules to keep spaces safe and on-topic. Humans do this work, but they're tired, inconsistent, and sometimes apply the wrong rule by mistake.
156.wh: The challenge isn't that humans are careless—it's that rules are often ambiguous. 'No harassment' means different things depending on context. Moderators work fast under cognitive load, so when they make a mistake, it's often by citing the wrong rule rather than using bad judgment. No one has a clear count of how wrong humans are, and fixing ambiguous rules is hard without systematic data.
156.ap: This study first shows that large language models can replicate human moderation decisions at 83.9% agreement. Then it evaluates real moderator decisions by having LLMs double-check them, uncovering that roughly 15% of removals and 13% of approvals are wrong. RuleSharpener uses LLMs to diagnose *why* errors happen—ambiguous rules, rules conflicting with community values—and generates clearer, more specific guidelines. These refined rules are then tested with moderators.
156.ww: Language models see patterns across thousands of decisions, so they can spot when a rule is being applied inconsistently. By flagging the root cause (ambiguous wording, conflicting guidance) rather than just saying 'this was wrong,' RuleSharpener points at what actually needs fixing. Clearer rules help moderators apply them consistently, which reduces errors.
156.po: RuleSharpener increased accuracy in identifying the violated rule by 38 percentage points. For platforms like Reddit, this translates to fewer user complaints, more consistent enforcement, and lower burden on moderators who no longer have to guess at murky standards. The system acts as a quality control tool that continuously improves the rules themselves.

157.bp: Depression is a serious mental health condition that's hard to catch early. If doctors could screen people based on what they post on social media, they might identify at-risk individuals sooner. But social media language is noisy and idiosyncratic—each person expresses distress differently.
157.wh: Most depression screening systems use a single fixed model and one reasoning approach, which doesn't adapt to the diversity of how people communicate symptoms. Social media data is scarce for mental health applications, so models trained on one dataset often fail on another. Different language models themselves might understand psychological symptoms differently, leading to inconsistent detection.
157.ap: AdaDepression uses two tricks. First, a two-hop retrieval: it collects representative posts from training data expressing depression symptoms, then uses these as anchors to find similar posts in a user's history—pulling out the symptom-relevant posts from their noise. Second, a Mixture of Routers mechanism that adapts both the reasoning strategy and the language model choice based on what it finds. If it retrieves lots of clear symptom expressions, it might use one model; if signals are mixed, another.
157.ww: Using representative posts as retrieval anchors works because people express similar psychological states in similar ways. The model learns what 'sadness looks like' in social media language, not just depression statistics. Adapting the reasoning strategy and model selection means the system doesn't force one approach—it can switch between direct reasoning, chain-of-thought, or other strategies depending on the data quality it finds.
157.po: The result is a screening framework that explicitly maps raw social media posts to standardized psychological questionnaires. For sparse-data users (those with few posts), this adaptive approach outperforms fixed-model systems. The payoff for public health is early identification of at-risk individuals so they can get help before crisis.

158.bp: Game studios make money from players spending real money in-game. Predicting which players will spend the most over their lifetime—their Lifetime Value—is crucial for targeting offers and budgeting marketing. The challenge is that spending is unpredictable: most players spend nothing, some spend a lot, and the distribution is messy.
158.wh: Player spending follows no simple pattern. Many players never spend (zero-inflation). Spending amounts are heavily skewed—a few whales spend enormous amounts while most spenders spend a little. Add in the complication that different games have different spending cultures, and you need to predict across multiple games at once with limited per-player data.
158.ap: DynaMoLTV models spending as a zero-inflated mixture of lognormal distributions—a statistical shape that can be zero (no spending), skewed (more small spenders than large), and heavy-tailed (occasional mega-spenders). It has a separate expert for each game to account for game-specific spending patterns. It also uses a hierarchical payment classifier to capture what kind of spender each player is. Two-stage losses balance identifying who will pay anything (binary classification) with predicting how much they'll spend (regression).
158.ww: Using the right distribution shape matters: lognormal is what real spending data looks like. Having game-specific experts prevents transfer learning disaster where a model trained on a hardcore player base predicts poorly for casual players. The two-stage approach makes sense because identifying a payer is a different problem than predicting a payer's total—the model learns both signals.
158.po: DynaMoLTV outperforms standard approaches on paid user identification, high-value user recall, and overall LTV prediction. For web-scale game monetization, this means studios can accurately target players most likely to spend, optimize marketing budgets per game, and predict revenue more reliably.

159.bp: Large language models are increasingly used for high-stakes decisions—healthcare advice, legal recommendations, financial planning—where being wrong is costly. But most benchmarks measure performance on friendly questions. Real-world decisions happen under pressure, time constraints, and confusing scenarios.
159.wh: Evaluating LLM reliability is hard because stress and constraints are hard to measure. A model might perform well on a simple question but fall apart when given a tight deadline, incomplete information, or conflicting requirements. Standard benchmarks miss this entirely, so models look reliable in the lab but fail in deployment.
159.ap: This study runs five increasingly difficult scenarios on three popular models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude). Each scenario is tested with a 45-item rubric checking accuracy, safety, logical consistency, and constraint-following. The Stress Sensitivity Index quantifies how much each model degrades as difficulty rises—measuring the slope of performance decline.
159.ww: This works because it mimics real deployment conditions: time limits force faster thinking, ambiguity forces interpretation, constraints force trade-offs. By measuring performance across a difficulty spectrum rather than a single easy benchmark, the rubric captures which models remain reliable under stress and which fall apart.
159.po: The results show ChatGPT remains stable, Gemini moderately degrades, and Claude shows substantial sensitivity—especially on constraint-following. For teams deploying LLMs in production, this stress-testing reveals which model will actually perform when it matters. Before shipping an LLM assistant to production, you need to know not just average performance but worst-case performance.

160.bp: Text-to-motion generation takes a description like 'a person dancing happily' and produces realistic human motion. Evaluating whether the motion is good requires metrics that measure how well the motion matches the text. Current metrics are flawed in ways that let researchers oversell mediocre work.
160.wh: Existing metrics like Fréchet Inception Distance assume data follows a bell curve, which motion data doesn't. Others like R-Precision are local—they only check if the top-ranking results match—and miss the global picture of whether the entire generated motion makes sense as a whole.
160.ap: The paper proposes two new metrics. Optimal Transport Matching Score treats text-to-motion matching as a routing problem: how do you pair each motion to a text description to maximize total similarity? This gives a global view. MoCLIP-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy uses an improved motion encoder (MoCLIP) and a Gaussian-RBF kernel to measure distribution differences without assuming bell-curve shapes.
160.ww: Optimal transport is a mathematical framework for comparing distributions globally—it sees the forest, not just trees. MoCLIP-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy avoids Gaussian assumptions by using kernel methods, which are more flexible. Both metrics align with human perception because they measure what humans actually care about: does the motion match the text overall, without bias from assumptions about data shape?
160.po: Models evaluated with these new metrics show stronger correlation with human judgment. For the text-to-motion generation field, this matters because it prevents researchers from claiming progress on unreliable benchmarks and guides actual improvement toward generating motions humans recognize as faithful to descriptions.

161.bp: Conversational search lets you ask questions back-and-forth with a search system, like talking to a librarian. You ask something vague, the librarian clarifies, refines their search, and eventually gives you what you need. This is more natural than typing keyword queries, especially for complex information needs.
161.wh: The hard part is understanding what you mean in context. If you say 'tell me more,' the system needs to know more about what. If you ask a follow-up that contradicts your first question, should the system assume you changed your mind or help you find both pieces of information? Conversational context is messy and requires real understanding, not just keyword matching.
161.ap: This is a tutorial covering conversational search from foundational principles to new agentic paradigms. Large language models enable this because they can generate natural responses, follow instructions to search strategically, and maintain context across turns. Agentic approaches add planning and dynamic retrieval—the system decides what to search for, when, and how to execute steps to fulfill complex requests.
161.ww: Language models understand conversation naturally; they avoid the brittle keyword-matching of older systems. Agentic capabilities mean the system can reason about what information would help you most, actively refining its strategy rather than just passively responding to your queries. This moves from 'answering your question' to 'helping you find what you need.'
161.po: Conversational search systems powered by these advances enable discovery workflows that feel more like talking to an expert than interacting with a database. Users get faster answers to complex questions and better-refined results because the system actively helps clarify rather than assuming your first phrasing was exactly what you meant.

162.bp: Companies want to understand how employees use AI assistants—which tasks get automated, how much time is saved, what roles change. This data is hidden in millions of multi-turn conversations between workers and their AI helpers.
162.wh: Raw multi-turn conversations are hard to analyze. One conversation might be a user asking for code help, then clarifying, then testing—all mixed together. Unsupervised clustering of raw text produces noise. You need summaries to see the intent, then topic structure to find patterns, and human judgment to ensure the patterns matter for business decisions.
162.ap: HILTON (Human-In-the-Loop Topic mOdeling) summarizes multi-turn conversations using language models to compress them into coherent summaries. It clusters these summaries into topics and organizes them hierarchically. Humans annotate and refine the clusters, giving feedback that improves future iterations. It trains a lightweight classifier on this refined data so new conversations can be automatically categorized.
162.ww: Summarization reduces noise and aligns the model with what humans care about (intent, not word choice). Human-in-the-loop feedback ensures topics are relevant to the business, not just mathematically coherent. The lightweight classifier lets the system scale—you can categorize thousands of conversations without expensive human review each time.
162.po: The result is a topic structure suitable for workplace analytics—understanding that 30% of assistant usage is debugging, 25% is documentation writing, etc. This data helps companies allocate training, design better tooling, and predict which roles will change most. Open-sourcing the code lets other organizations apply the same approach.

163.bp: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts your files and demands payment. Modern detection uses machine learning on behavioral telemetry—logs of what programs do. But privacy laws now require the ability to delete your data from trained models without retraining from scratch.
163.wh: Standard model training stores information from all training samples throughout the model. Deleting one sample usually means retraining the entire model from scratch, which is expensive. For large security systems protecting millions of machines, retraining is prohibitively slow. You need a way to 'unlearn' specific samples efficiently.
163.ap: SISA training partitions the dataset into shards (independent chunks). Models are trained separately on each shard and then combined. When you need to delete a sample, you only retrain the shard containing it, not the entire model. The study tests this on reinforcement learning models trained to detect ransomware using behavioral data. Detection confidence is measured continuously (Q-score margins) rather than just binary predictions.
163.ww: Sharding works because the model's knowledge is compartmentalized—each shard contributes independently. When you retrain one shard, the others stay the same. This dramatically reduces recomputation. Continuous confidence scoring is more realistic than binary decisions because security is about confidence levels, not hard yes/no calls.
163.po: SISA unlearning achieves 5-10x faster deletion than retraining the whole model, while maintaining detection performance. For ransomware detection systems protecting enterprises, this means compliance with data deletion requests is fast and affordable, enabling responsible AI deployment where privacy rights are respected without sacrificing security.

164.bp: Drug development requires predicting which new molecules will cause side effects. Each drug is represented as a graph—atoms and bonds form a structure. Some side effects have been observed and reported, but most are simply unknown. You need to identify the unknown dangerous ones.
164.wh: The problem is that positive drugs (known side effects) and negative drugs (unknown side effects) might look structurally similar. A harmless drug and a dangerous drug might both contain similar substructures, making it hard to tell them apart. Without explicit negative examples, the model lacks guidance on what patterns distinguish truly dangerous drugs. This is called positive-unlabeled classification.
164.ap: Delta-PU performs dual reweighting on graphs. Hop-level reweighting emphasizes important substructures during pooling—the process that combines information from different atomic neighborhoods into a graph representation. Graph-level reweighting suppresses ambiguous unlabeled graphs from influencing training. The model learns to focus on discriminative structural patterns while reducing the noise from uncertain examples.
164.ww: Reweighting substructures rather than treating all atoms equally lets the model discover what structural features distinguish side effects. Reweighting graphs reduces the model's confusion about which unlabeled drugs are truly negative versus genuinely ambiguous. By progressively focusing on discriminative patterns, the model avoids overfitting to noise.
164.po: Delta-PU achieves state-of-the-art performance on drug side effect prediction and other positive-unlabeled graph classification tasks. For pharmaceutical research, this means more accurate predictions of dangerous molecular structures from limited labeled data, potentially speeding drug safety assessment.
